evidence_summary: 56% said Canada accepts too many immigrants in 2025; police-reported anti-South-Asian hate crimes reached 483 in 2025 (+49% YoY); immigration levels were sharply reduced and the debate is increasingly politicized. Scores are ordinal coding, not per-capita incidence.

2025 polling found 69% considered overall migration too high and 41% said its overall impact had mostly been bad; immigration was a top issue in 2026; graduate permission is due to reduce to 18 months for applications from 2027. Asian ethnicity appears in 33% of racially/religiously aggravated crimes where victim ethnicity was recorded, but victim-ethnicity coverage is incomplete.

Gallup found 73% of U.S. adults still said immigration was good for the country in June 2026 (29% wanted it decreased); separately, a representative AAPI survey found 49% experienced a race/ethnicity/nationality-based hate act in 2025 and 53% reported themselves or someone they knew was negatively affected by immigration-policy changes or anti-immigrant sentiment. AAPI is a broad proxy and not Indian-specific.

2025 Australia-India survey found 44% of respondents thought discrimination against Indian Australians was frequent or very frequent (58% among Indian Australians; 43% among non-Indian Australians). Australia retains strong broad support for multiculturalism, while concerns about immigration levels and student-visa settings are material. The public-sentiment code reflects mixed—not uniformly hostile—views.

The 2026 social-cohesion report says 36% considered recent immigration too high, but 67% agreed multiculturalism is good and 54% saw immigrants as good for the economy; 22% of Asian respondents in the 2025 survey wave reported discrimination in the prior 12 months. The India–New Zealand FTA entering into force on 20 October 2026 adds specific Indian visa commitments.

Eurobarometer found 73% agreed immigrants contribute positively to Ireland; immigration-related concern is rising, with housing a much larger concern. Insufficient comparable evidence on India-specific hostility and current pathway friction for a composite score.

Japan's official survey of foreign residents found 15.9% of dissatisfied respondents cited discrimination against foreigners as a reason for dissatisfaction; a separate FY2022 survey reported 15% of foreign residents had experienced hate speech. The latter is not India-specific and the sample/report years differ from other countries.

Official rules say third-country nationals generally must be highly qualified, permits are limited, and employers must show no suitable Swiss/EU/EFTA candidate. This is high structural policy friction, not evidence of anti-Indian public hostility.
Hong Kong has active talent-admission schemes including a 2025 channel for selected skilled trades; there is not yet comparable survey evidence here on anti-immigrant or anti-Indian sentiment.
